nameStory: The Eurasian Running Crab Spider gets its name from its sideways, crab-like movement and its incredible speed when hunting or escaping danger. Unlike web-building spiders that wait patiently in one spot, these athletic arachnids are constantly on the move, darting across tree bark and leaves with surprising agility. The 'Eurasian' part hints at its Old World origins, though it has found its way to New England forests.
description: This is a small, agile hunter that looks quite different depending on whether you're seeing a male or female. The males are striking with their shiny, iridescent black or dark brown bodies edged in white, almost like they're wearing tiny tuxedos. Females are more variable in both size and color, ranging from browns to grays. At about 5mm long (roughly the size of a pencil eraser), these spiders are active predators that hunt without webs, instead relying on their speed and stealth.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Flattened, crab-like body that's wider than it is tall, with legs that extend sideways rather than straight out - you'll notice it can scuttle sideways just like a tiny crab

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Males have distinctive shiny black or dark brown coloring with crisp white edges that catch the light, while females show more muted, variable browns and grays

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small at about 5mm long - roughly the width of a pencil eraser - but appears larger when legs are extended sideways

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Extremely quick and agile, often seen darting across bark or leaves in short, rapid bursts before freezing motionless in perfect camouflage

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No web at all - these are pure hunters that rely on ambush tactics, remaining perfectly still until prey comes within striking distance

habitat: Look for these spiders on the bark of trees and shrubs throughout New England's mixed and deciduous forests. They prefer the textured surfaces of oak, maple, and birch trees where their camouflaged colors blend perfectly with the bark patterns. You might also spot them on larger bushes and understory plants, always positioned where they can ambush passing flies and small insects.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging to hunt on sun-warmed bark surfaces during mild afternoons.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both males and females are most visible, with mating occurring and the distinctive male coloration at its most vibrant.
seasonality.fall: Females may be seen with egg sacs, and activity continues until the first hard frosts arrive.
seasonality.winter: Adults seek shelter under loose bark or in crevices, becoming dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: These spiders are like tiny chameleons of the spider world - they can remain so perfectly motionless that they seem to disappear into tree bark, but when they decide to move, they can sprint faster than almost any other spider their size, covering distances several times their body length in the blink of an eye.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other running crab spiders in the same family, but the male's distinctive shiny black coloration with white edges is quite unique. Remember: 'Tuxedo male, plain Jane female' - if you see that formal black-and-white pattern, you've likely found a male Eurasian Running Crab Spider.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Eurasian,' this spider is now established in North America, showing how some introduced species can quietly integrate into local ecosystems. The name 'crab spider' is used for several different spider families, which can be confusing - these running crab spiders are different from the more common flower crab spiders that sit motionless on blooms.
compareHints: Among its Philodromus relatives in New England, the male's distinctive shiny black coloration with white edges makes it relatively easy to distinguish from the more uniformly colored Metallic Crab Spider or the striped patterns of the White-striped Running Crab Spider. The females are trickier, but this species tends to be found more consistently on tree bark rather than on flowers or low vegetation like some of its cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the White-striped Running Crab Spider which has obvious white stripes, the metallic crab spider males are uniformly shiny without stripes.

The white-striped running crab spider is distinguished from its relatives by those prominent longitudinal white stripes - most other Philodromus species in New England have more subtle markings or different color patterns.

The Turf Running Spider differs from its Philodromus relatives primarily in habitat preference - while the Metallic Crab Spider tends toward trees and the White-striped Running Crab Spider prefers taller shrubs, the Turf Running Spider sticks to low vegetation and ground cover.

Compared to other Philodromus species in New England, the Resplendent Running Crab Spider stands out for its particularly brilliant metallic appearance - more lustrous than the Metallic Crab Spider and lacking the white stripes of the White-striped Running Crab Spider.
The Minute Running Crab Spider is significantly smaller than its relatives like the Metallic Crab Spider or White-striped Running Crab Spider, which are much more commonly encountered.
Philodromus exilis is notably more slender than the Metallic Crab Spider or White-striped Running Crab Spider, lacking the metallic sheen or distinct striping of those relatives.
